newsitem.title: USA: Commonwealth agrees on Nigeria mission - reports.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth agrees on Nigeria mission - reports.

text.p: Commonwealth ministers discussing how to push Nigeria back onto the road to democracy have agreed in principle to send a fact-finding mission to the powerful oil-rich African state, delegates said on Sunday.

"We have agreed to send a mission to Nigeria. Now we have to work out the conditions," one delegate told reporters ahead of the second day of talks on how to tackle Nigeria, which was suspended from the 53-nation grouping last November.

The delegates' comments seemed to indicate that the eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group had decided to give Nigeria another chance rather than imposing a set of sanctions that were agreed on but have been suspended since April.
Ministers arriving at the New York meeting took a more cautious line, however, saying many details had to be worked out before a concrete decision could be taken on sending a delegation.

"We are discussing this as well as what other measures could be taken," said Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, a long-time proponent of taking a hard line against the government of General Sani Abacha.
A Commonwealth spokesman said the talks, held in the Malaysian mission to the United Nations, were expected to end at around 1 p.m. EDT (1700 GMT).

The Commonwealth, a grouping of Britain and its former colonies and protectorates, suspended the populous west African nation in November after the execution of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority-rights activists.

The ministerial action group has already tried to send one fact-finding mission to Nigeria but scrapped the idea last month after Abuja refused to let it meet human rights campaigners and opposition groups.

Axworthy said on Friday that it would be pointless to send a mission to Nigeria if it were restricted to meeting officials, but other action group states say that some sort of dialogue has to be maintained with Abuja.

Nigeria seems unlikely to change its mind about the scope of an action group mission, leaving Commonwealth ministers with the tricky task of setting a mandate for the delegation that would satisfy both sides.
Nigeria insists on discussing its suspension from the Commonwealth before broaching other topics.

Axworthy's frustration with what he saw as foot-dragging by other members over Nigeria boiled over a few days ago when he denounced "appeasers" in the grouping, but a Commonwealth spokesman said participants had kept their tempers so far.

In June Axworthy said Canada would unilaterally impose the sanctions the action group had agreed on -- including a ban on sports links and arms sales -- but experts said the only measure to have any effect would be an worldwide embargo on oil sales.

Britain and New Zealand oppose the idea on the grounds that it would hurt ordinary Nigerians. And an embargo would only work with the support of the United States, which buys 40 percent of its oil from Nigeria.
The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group consists of Malaysia, Zimbabwe, Jamaica, Ghana, Britain, New Zealand, South Africa and Canada.
